Agent cost preview for Sim · case study · 2026-11-25

Agent Cost Preview — Process & Iteration

How a missing feature in Sim (sim.ai) became a working tool: what an AI agent will cost per month, and what drives that cost, before it is deployed. Built in two iterations. The second came from comparing the estimate with 6 real runs in Sim. Real screenshots of each version, with the changes circled in red.

00

The problem and the design decision

Steps A to DSim, then a one-page spec

The Problem

Sim shows what an agent run cost only after it has run, as one total per run. A builder who needs budget approval has to spend credits on test runs, then rebuild the monthly figure in a spreadsheet — and still can't tell which block drives the bill.

Today, with Sim and a spreadsheetWith the cost preview
1. Run the agent on sample inputs (credits, or an API key)1. Pick a preset or describe the blocks
2. Open each run's log, one at a time2. Enter the runs per month
3. Read each run's total (no breakdown)3. Read and copy the 5-line summary
4. Look up token prices on the provider's site (BYOK)3 actions instead of 7: −57%. No run, no credits, no key. The biggest cost driver is named in 100% of estimates.
5. Spreadsheet: average × monthly volume
6. Guess which block drives the cost
7. Write the business case by hand

The Design Decision

Levers first: one sentence naming what drives the cost, then one monthly figure with its range, then "what if" (volume ×2, cheaper model, fewer loops). The figure comes before any run — and a few real runs pasted from Sim's logs turn the estimate into a calibrated one.

Deliberately Tight Scope

  • 1 page, 3 actions, 2 presets (an email agent at ~$5 a month, a research agent at ~$235 a month)
  • No Sim account, no API key, no backend: everything runs in the browser. No change to Sim's interface
  • Goal: prove a cost can be predicted before deploying, within ±20% of real runs — not ship a full product
01

Iteration 1: from the v0 draft to a working V2

v0Claude CodeStep E · spec from step D

v0 generated the layout and a first version of the logic from a one-page brief. Reviewing it found two calculation bugs. The logic was rewritten as pure functions with tests, and the results were reordered as the spec asked.

  • 1Driver first, in large type: the sentence saying what drives the cost now opens the results. In the draft it was a small grey line above a table.
  • 2One figure instead of a 5-column table: the monthly cost and its range, readable at a glance by a budget owner.
  • 3BYOK bug fixed: with your own keys, the draft's monthly total ($5.00) left out the model provider's bill. V2 shows both bills together: 1,000 Sim credits + $0.41 to the provider.
  • 4"Half the loop iterations" removed when there is no loop: it showed the same cost as today and added noise.
  • 5Workflow import added: paste a Sim workflow export (JSON) to fill the blocks. Optional, best-effort.
  • Not visible in a screenshot: calibration gave every block the same token counts, which broke workflows with several blocks. Fixed, and 11 tests added.
02

Iteration 2: what 6 real runs in Sim changed

Real runs in SimSteps F and G · gemini-3.5-flash-lite, your own key, free plan

This is where the real thinking happened. I ran the email agent 6 times in Sim and compared every number with the estimate. The total was right (+4%), but for the wrong reason: Sim's base fee is 97% of this agent's cost. The model's part was off by 120%.

BeforeAfterWhy
One guessed answer length (120 tokens)Short + long answer, with a shareReal answers ran from 22 to 90 tokens: urgent emails get a summary, the others don't
Calibrate on 1 real run3 to 5 runs, averagedCalibrating on one run still left a 47% error
Range: ±10% around one runCheapest to dearest run5 of 6 real runs fell outside the old range
Failed runs not mentionedNote9 failed runs cost 1 credit each, even those that failed in 30 ms
BYOK cost read from Sim's logsNoteWith your own key, Sim logs the model cost as $0
gemini-2.5-flash-lite offeredRemovedStill in Sim's list, but Google refuses it to new users (404)
  • 1Answer length per branch: each block has a typical answer and a long answer with the share of inputs that get it. Error on answer length: +177% → −17%.
  • 2Calibration on several runs: one run per line, pasted from Sim's logs. The badge says how many runs it uses.
  • 3What Sim doesn't show: failed runs are charged, and with your own key the model cost is $0 in Sim's logs.
  • 4A range that holds the real runs: it now goes from the cheapest to the dearest real run. Real runs inside the range: 1 of 6 → 6 of 6.
  • Not visible in a screenshot: without calibration, the low end of the range is now −70% on the answer (it was −30%), and the retired Gemini model is gone from the list.

Both shots use gpt-4.1-mini prices with the real token counts. Under these prices, 1 of the 6 real runs falls in V2's range, and all 6 fall in V3's: by design, since V3's range runs from the cheapest to the dearest run.

What this demonstrates, and where it stands

Live: costly-silk.vercel.app
Not just the ability to prototype a tool — the ability to test my own numbers against reality and redesign around what broke (answer length per branch, a range that holds the real runs, charges the product doesn't show), and to say plainly when an estimate was right for the wrong reason.
  • Works now: estimate without running, calibrate with real runs, two bills in BYOK, plan fit, a copyable summary for the budget owner. 14 tests pass; the live page shows the same figures as the local build.
  • Still to do: show the summary to 3 people who never used Sim, and the prototype to 5 builders (stop if fewer than 3 say they needed it). Check the JSON import against a real Sim export.
  • Where it would live in Sim: a pre-deploy check next to the Deploy button. Not built: this project doesn't change Sim's interface.
  • Live Demo: https://costly-silk.vercel.app
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/fnnysimon/projects/tree/main/sim-agent-testing
